content.title: About
content.content: Almond oil is obtained from almond (Prunus dulcis) seeds by cold pressing. It has a light nutty aroma, pale‑yellow color, and a delicate texture. The oil is used in cooking, cosmetics, and aromatherapy.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Almond oil is rich in vitamin E, a powerful antioxidant.
Unlike many vegetable oils, almond oil contains a higher proportion of monounsaturated fats.
Traditionally, it has been used in the Mediterranean region for skin and hair care.
Cold‑pressed oil retains most of the beneficial compounds, whereas refined oil loses aroma and many nutrients.
Its mild, sweet scent makes it a popular base in aromatic blends.

items.title: Skin support
items.content: Vitamin E and fatty acids help moisturize the skin, reduce dryness, and aid the healing of minor irritations.

items.title: Antioxidant protection
items.content: Antioxidants protect cells from oxidative stress, which may slow aging processes.

items.title: Heart health
items.content: Monounsaturated fats can help lower LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Hair nourishment
items.content: The oil feeds hair follicles, making hair shinier and more resilient.

items.title: Digestive aid
items.content: Small amounts can improve the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Tree nut allergy
items.content: People allergic to almonds may react to even tiny amounts of the oil.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The oil is very calorie‑dense; excessive use can contribute to weight gain.

items.title: Possible impurities
items.content: Low‑quality oil may contain solvent residues or be highly refined, reducing its beneficial properties.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Add almond oil to salads, dressings, smoothies, and baked goods. In cosmetics it is used as a moisturizing massage or night oil, as well as for hair and nail care.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dark place. After opening, store in the refrigerator and use within 3‑6 months. Discard if it develops a rancid smell.

content.title: About
content.content: Barley groats are made from crushed kernels of barley (Hordeum vulgare) that have had the outer hull removed. They retain more fiber than polished pearl barley. When cooked, barley groats are soft and crumbly with a light nutty flavor. They are cooked as porridge and used in soups, stews, and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Barley is one of the oldest cereal crops, grown for thousands of years.
Barley groats are crushed kernels, while pearl barley is whole kernels polished to a rounded shape.
Pearl barley is named for its resemblance to pearls.
Barley is rich in beta-glucans, a type of soluble fiber.
Barley is also made into malt, which is used to brew beer.

items.title: Contain beta-glucans
items.content: Beta-glucans are a soluble fiber that may help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: Slow carbohydrates
items.content: Thanks to fiber, barley groats raise blood sugar more slowly than many other grains.

items.title: Contain magnesium and selenium
items.content: These minerals support muscle and nerve function and immunity.

items.title: Contain B vitamins
items.content: Thiamine and niacin help the body get energy from food.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Barley contains gluten and is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten intolerance.

items.title: Bloating
items.content: The fiber and fructans in barley cause gas in some people.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Allergy to barley and other grains is possible.

items.title: Carbohydrates
items.content: Barley groats are rich in carbohydrates, so people with diabetes should watch their portion.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rinse the groats, soak them for a few hours if you like, and cook in water in a ratio of about 1 to 3 for about 30–45 minutes until tender. Serve as porridge and a side dish, or add them to soups, stews, casseroles, and salads; they go well with mushrooms and vegetables.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store groats in an airtight container in a dry, cool, dark place. Keep cooked groats in the refrigerator for three to five days.

content.title: About
content.content: Rotisserie chicken drumsticks are a popular dish worldwide. The skin stays on, keeping the meat juicy and adding a flavorful crispy layer. They are commonly served at street stalls, fast‑food restaurants, and family picnics.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rotisserie cooking allows the meat to turn evenly, basting itself in its own juices and fat.
Chicken skin contains collagen, which becomes gelatinous when cooked properly and can be beneficial for joints.
The tradition of rotisserie chicken originated in the Mediterranean and spread globally.
A blend of spices such as paprika, garlic, and rosemary enhances aroma and makes the skin extra crunchy.
Chicken drumsticks are often featured in cooking contests because they are easy to prepare and versatile for marinades.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Chicken meat provides a complete source of protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Drumsticks contain niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, supporting metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of minerals
items.content: Iron, zinc, and phosphorus are present in the meat and skin, important for blood health and bones.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Chicken drumsticks fit well into low‑carb diets as they contain virtually no sugars.

items.title: Collagen in the skin
items.content: When cooked correctly, the skin retains collagen, which may support skin elasticity and joint health.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to chicken meat or skin.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: The skin adds saturated and monounsaturated fats; people monitoring fat intake should consume in moderation.

items.title: Bacterial contamination risk
items.content: Improper cooking can leave salmonella or campylobacter alive.

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: Pre‑made marinades are often high in salt, which can be an issue for hypertension.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat the drumstick whole, pulling the meat off the bone. The skin is eaten crispy, while the meat stays juicy. It pairs well with barbecue sauce, mustard, or yogurt‑based dips. If the skin feels too fatty, it can be removed before eating.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked drumsticks in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a bag at –18 °C for up to 2 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of 75 °C before consumption.

content.title: About
content.content: Full Throttle is an energy drink designed to boost physical and mental performance. It contains caffeine, taurine, B‑vitamins, and sugar (or sugar substitutes in the diet version). Available in flavors such as "Pomegranate", "Apple‑Cinnamon" and "Strawberry‑Lemon".

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Full Throttle was first launched in 2005 as part of Monster Beverage's product line.
The brand markets itself as "for those who live at full speed" and frequently sponsors extreme sports events.
The formula includes taurine, an amino acid commonly used in energy drinks to support the nervous system.
In some markets a sugar‑free version is sold, sweetened with sucralose and acesulfame‑K.
The label typically lists caffeine content at 160 mg per 473 ml can.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Caffeine stimulates the central nervous system, increasing alertness and reducing perceived fatigue.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: B‑vitamins help convert food into usable energy, supporting a more efficient metabolism.

items.title: Improved focus
items.content: Taurine may aid cognitive function and reaction time during high‑intensity activities.

items.title: Excess caffeine intake
items.content: High caffeine doses can cause anxiety, insomnia, rapid heartbeat, and elevated blood pressure.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Sugared versions can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries if consumed frequently.

items.title: Not for children or pregnant women
items.content: Due to its high caffeine level, the drink is not recommended for children, adolescents, pregnant or nursing women.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Drink Full Throttle chilled, straight from the can. Limit consumption to 1‑2 cans per day. Do not mix with alcohol.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Once opened, consume within 3‑5 days for best quality.

content.title: About
content.content: Black olives are the ripe fruits of the olive tree (Olea europaea) that are typically fermented in brine or a marinade. They have a mild, slightly salty flavor, a meaty texture, and a characteristic dark purple‑black color.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black olives are produced from green olives by additional fermentation, not by natural ripening.
The olive tree has been a symbol of peace and victory in ancient Greece and Rome.
Olive oil, extracted from olives, is a cornerstone of the Mediterranean diet.
In ancient Rome olives were used as a form of payment and as diplomatic gifts.
Black olives are commonly served as a snack alongside wine and cheese platters.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Black olives contain polyphenols such as oleuropein that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Monounsaturated fats in olive oil help lower LDL‑cholesterol levels.

items.title: Contains vitamin E
items.content: Vitamin E acts as an antioxidant, protecting cell membranes and supporting immune function.

items.title: Source of iron and copper
items.content: These minerals are involved in hemoglobin formation and energy metabolism.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The fiber in olives promotes regular bowel movements.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Because black olives are often cured in brine, excessive consumption can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Olive allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to olives or olive oil.

items.title: Oleuropein sensitivity
items.content: In large amounts, oleuropein can cause gastrointestinal discomfort.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Black olives can be enjoyed as a snack, added to salads, pastas, pizza, tapas, or used in sauces and marinades. They are often served in oil with herbs or in a wine‑vinegar brine.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep olives in their original brine in a sealed jar in the refrigerator. Properly stored, they last several months. Discard any olives that develop mold, off‑odors, or an off‑taste.

content.title: About
content.content: Seafood soufflé is a light baked dish made from eggs, cream, cheese and a mix of seafood such as shrimp, mussels, salmon or crab meat. It has an airy texture, a delicate marine aroma and can be served as an appetizer or a main course.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Soufflé originates from French cuisine, where the word means “blown up”.
The airy structure comes from beaten egg whites that create bubbles during baking.
Seafood soufflé is often presented in small ceramic ramekins to keep its shape.
In Japan a version with nori seaweed is popular, adding a subtle umami flavor.
A soufflé can collapse if the oven is opened too early or the temperature drops suddenly.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Seafood and eggs provide high‑quality protein essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Fatty fish like salmon contain EPA and DHA, which support heart and brain health.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Eggs and seafood are rich in B12, riboflavin and niacin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Seafood soufflé supplies zinc, selenium and iodine, which aid immune function and thyroid health.

items.title: Low in carbs
items.content: The dish fits low‑carb diets as its main energy sources are protein and fat.

items.title: Seafood allergy
items.content: People allergic to shrimp, mussels or fish may experience severe reactions to seafood soufflé.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Eggs and seafood contain cholesterol; individuals with high cholesterol should monitor portion size.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Improperly stored seafood can harbor bacteria and toxins, so always use fresh ingredients.

items.title: Over‑cooking
items.content: Soufflé can become dry if baked too long, losing its characteristic lightness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve seafood soufflé immediately after baking while it is still puffed. Garnish with fresh herbs, a squeeze of lemon, or a light cream sauce. Pair with a simple salad or crusty bread.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2 days. Reheat in the oven at 150 °C for 10–15 minutes to restore texture before serving.
